meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.reviewer: Automated open-source review (daily, see docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md); first run seeded by the 23 Sep 2026 open-source review. Items marked unverified need confirmation. Timelines researched from open sources on 24 Sep 2026.
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

1.name: Priority Conflicts
1.desc: High relevance to the Army — followed every week in the brief.

2.name: Active Regional & Escalation Watches
2.desc: Regional theatres where escalation would change Singapore's or the Army's picture.

3.name: Baseline Regional Research Reserve
3.desc: Held for pattern and case-study value; reviewed on trigger or on the monthly cycle.

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

Active.desc: Material trend, escalation, or regional relevance.

Watch.desc: Baseline monitoring; no current learning priority.

Archive.desc: Reserve — retained for reference and pattern work; revisit only on a named trigger.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch (named event, threshold, deadline, mobilisation sign, force movement, diplomatic decision or escalation indicator). Expand the row for the full list and what each would mean.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.

items.name: Russia–Ukraine

phase.now: Attritional stalemate; reciprocal deep-strike war; Ukraine regaining local initiative

snapshots.phase: Attritional war
Attritional stalemate; reciprocal deep-strike war; Ukraine regaining local initiative

items.whyNow: Richest adaptation feed on the list: Russia industrialised jet-powered Geran-4/5 strikes (~3,000 in August, interception rate down to ~87%), Ukraine ran record-range refinery strikes and a 1,110-drone raid on Moscow, and Operation Vivaldi restored local manoeuvre at Lyman — while an energy-strike truce claimed by Trump at UNGA is unconfirmed by Kyiv.
changes: Russia's strike architecture shifted to jet-powered drones: ~1,500 jet Gerans used in July and ~3,000 in August (56% of August packages), Ukrainian interception rates fell from ~92% to ~87%; Ukraine is field-testing four turbojet interceptors (ISW/Critical Threats 1 Sep).

Ukraine's deep-strike campaign reached record range (Tyumen refinery ~2,000 km, 25 Jul; more than 12 refinery strikes 2–24 Aug; Astrakhan gas plant 24 Aug), Operation MoLoChKa hit 100+ shadow-fleet vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea (July), and a 1,110-drone raid struck Moscow's refinery on 20 Sep; Russia answered with a 212-drone and missile barrage as UNGA opened.

Ground: Russia seized only ~90 km² in August (505 km² a year earlier) for ~42,000 casualties; it holds ~72% of Kostiantynivka and is 12–13 km from Sloviansk–Kramatorsk while repositioning armour to Dobropillia; Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps confirmed Operation Vivaldi (15 Sep), clearing ~85 km² north-west of Lyman.

Leadership and mobilisation: Defence Minister Fedorov replaced by Khmara and Syrskyi by Maj Gen Drapatyi as C-in-C (15–22 Jul) amid protests; Russia recruits ~27,000 a month against 30,000+ losses with street round-ups from 10 Aug and Ukrainian intelligence reporting preparations for a 600,000-strong mobilisation.

Diplomacy: Witkoff and Kushner saw Putin (5 Sep) and Zelensky (6 Sep) without a deal; Budanov says a trilateral round is being prepared for October; at UNGA (22 Sep) Trump claimed an energy-strike halt that Kyiv says it was not informed of; EU adopted the 21st sanctions package (23 Jul) and rolled over ~3,000 listings (22 Sep). Romania's airspace was violated 23 times in 2026; NATO condemned incursions on 12 Aug.

timeline.text: A Russian drone strike on a munitions warehouse in Myla, near Kyiv, set off explosions that killed 38 people, the deadliest single attack in Ukraine in 2026.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three-hour talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against both capitals.
Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the pause declared during the US envoys' visit.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.
Ukrainian drones set fire to the Yaroslavl refinery's primary crude unit and destroyed transport aircraft and helicopters at Rostov-on-Don airfield, Ukraine's General Staff said.
A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, halting processing for several weeks, Reuters reported citing industry sources.
Ukraine struck the Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa and the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara overnight, both more than 900 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, causing fires.
Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly, said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and urged trilateral talks with Putin at the G20 in Miami.

status.summary: Front lines are largely static, but both sides are striking deep: Russia with mass jet-drone attacks on Ukraine's grid and industry, Ukraine with record-range strikes on Russian refineries and gas plants and a 1,110-drone raid on Moscow. A US-led talks track is live (a trilateral round is being prepared for October) while Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi claws back ground near Lyman.

items.name: Israel–Palestine (Gaza)

phase.now: Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted raids

snapshots.phase: Phase 1 ceasefire, unresolved disarmament
Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted raids

items.whyNow: The October 2025 truce formally holds but nothing in it is being implemented: Hamas accepted the Board of Peace roadmap and dissolved its governing committee, Israel rejected the roadmap and holds 65–70% of Gaza behind a lethally enforced Yellow Line while running decapitation raids. The October ISF pilot and the 27 Oct Israeli election decide the next phase.
changes: Hamas dissolved its Government Emergency Committee (6 Jul), ceding civil administration to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, which Israel has blocked from entering; the Board of Peace issued a 15-point roadmap (30–31 Jul: phased decommissioning, verification committee, phased IDF withdrawal) that Hamas accepted and Netanyahu rejected on 9 Aug ('no withdrawal until real, not fictitious, disarmament').

The security cabinet approved a ~200-troop International Stabilisation Force pilot at Rafah (26–27 Jul) on condition the IDF keeps the Yellow Line; Uganda's parliament approved ~1,200 troops (7 Aug) for an October deployment now 'in doubt', Morocco (up to 500) is first to deploy with a 150-person outpost under construction, Kosovo and Albania signed on, Indonesia's ~8,000 are suspended.

IDF control rose to 65–70% of Gaza (Crisis Group, Aug) from 53% at the ceasefire; Yellow Line pushed toward the sea and lethally enforced; a US official noted tighter strike-approval rules (6 Aug) but 24 Aug strikes hit a desalination plant, a mosque and an aid warehouse.

Targeted operations replaced manoeuvre: special forces captured Hamas internal-security chief Muein al-Arabeed in Gaza City (1 Sep; Hamas warned the truce could 'break down completely'); an airstrike killed Khan Younis Brigade commander Muhammad al-Yazouri and a company commander (10–11 Sep).

Humanitarian baseline worsened: Kerem Shalom is the sole cargo crossing since Zikim closed (24 May), WFP halved rations to 200,000, the population is confined to about a third of the Strip; ~1,390 killed since the ceasefire (73,910 since October 2023) and four IDF soldiers; Cairo talks stalled on weapons.

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
An Israeli-backed raid in Gaza City detained the head of Hamas's internal security service; airstrikes covering the withdrawal killed at least five Palestinians, including two children.
US envoy Jared Kushner said Israel's 27 October election was making its government 'a little irrational' on Gaza, as the Board of Peace disarmament plan stalled.
Kosovo signed a Participating Country Agreement for the International Stabilization Force in Pristina, while Board of Peace envoy Mladenov admitted implementation was 'not there yet'.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.
An Israeli airstrike on a vehicle in Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan and another man; Palestinian officials count 1,400 killed since the ceasefire.

A first international stabilisation contingent was meant to enter Rafah in October but is now in doubt.

items.name: US–Israel–Iran

phase.now: Blockade-and-attrition stalemate; Hormuz effectively closed; UNGA opening

snapshots.phase: Post-war MOU under a fragile stand-down
Blockade-and-attrition stalemate; Hormuz effectively closed; UNGA opening

items.whyNow: An active war over sea-lane access: the MOU lapsed, the US port blockade is back, Hormuz transits are in single digits on most counts, an IRGC salvo targeted a US carrier group and the US answered 'tanker for tanker' — while the first mediated face-to-face session (22 Sep) opened a diplomatic window that Trump ties to the November midterms. Highest Singapore-exposure item: more than half of Singapore's crude imports come through the Gulf and a Singapore-flagged ship was hit in June.
changes: The stand-down collapsed on 7–9 Jul (Iran struck three ships; the US revoked Iran's oil-sale licence and hit 90 targets), the naval blockade was reinstated on 14 Jul, Iranian missiles killed two US soldiers at Muwaffaq Salti (18–19 Jul) and IRGC strikes hit Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Erbil (24 Jul) before a mutual pause on 25–26 Jul; the 60-day Islamabad MOU lapsed on 17 Aug with no deal (transits 3 a day, ~520 ships stranded, Iranian exports down to 156 kb/d).

Kinetic resumption: US strikes on IRGC mine-rocket launchers on Larak Island (30 Aug) and rebuilt coastal radars (1–2 Sep); IRGC fire at bases in Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq; on 5 Sep an IRGC ballistic salvo targeted the USS George Washington group (evaded) and ~32 missiles damaged eight F-15s and an A-10 at Muwaffaq Salti; the US disabled the tankers Downy and Stark 1 and sank Kylo ('tanker for tanker').

Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab: CENTCOM cleared 100+ suspected mines (25 Aug) but two tankers were hit by unknown projectiles on 21 Sep; Lloyd's List counted 97 non-Iranian transits in the week of 7–13 Sep (a three-week high) against a pre-war ~85–138 a day, PortWatch shows 1–3 a day; war-risk cover ~40× pre-crisis; Houthis with IRGC officers seized Mokha, Perim and Hanish (10 Sep), 70 km from the Bab al-Mandab lanes.

Iran and Oman exchanged Hormuz management proposals (28 Jul: Oman a Malacca-style voluntary fee, Iran a ~$1m per-vessel charge with Iranian mine clearance); Washington: 'we don't want tolls'; the IAEA Board referred Iran to the Security Council on 9 Sep, the first referral in 20 years.

Diplomacy: Iran sent terms via Qatar (19 Sep: end the war on all fronts, unfreeze assets, lift the blockade; reopening 'within 7 days' if the blockade eases); a three-hour mediated Araghchi–Witkoff–Kushner session on 22 Sep was called 'promising, constructive'; Trump told UNGA a deal comes 'right after the election' or he will 'annihilate'; Pezeshkian addressed UNGA on 23 Sep. Singapore: MHA cites more than half of crude imports from the Middle East; the Singapore-flagged Ever Lovely was struck on 25 Jun (MPA).

history.note: Baseline: Hormuz crisis, direct Singapore exposure.

timeline.text: The US and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lifted the US naval blockade, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and opened a 60-day negotiating period.
After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.
US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people, including five at a wedding in Kuhestak; the IRGC answered with missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait.
After the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.
US forces struck five Iranian tankers after Iran attacked ten ships near Hormuz and fired 20 ballistic missiles at Jordan's Al-Azraq base, 18 of them intercepted.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted the port blockade.
Witkoff and Kushner held three hours of Qatari-mediated indirect talks with Iran's foreign minister in New York, as Trump told the UN he could 'annihilate' Iran absent a deal.
The bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit by an unknown projectile off Musandam in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one Indian crew member, UKMTO and Omani authorities reported.

status.summary: An active war over the Strait of Hormuz: the US blockade is back, transits are a fraction of normal, and in early September the two sides traded a missile salvo at a US carrier group and 'tanker-for-tanker' strikes. The first mediated face-to-face talks took place at the UN on 22 September; Trump ties any deal to after the November midterms.

items.name: Israel–Lebanon

phase.now: Framework in name; attritional occupation of a self-declared security zone

snapshots.phase: Active ceasefire with daily fighting
Framework in name; attritional occupation of a self-declared security zone

items.whyNow: The Trilateral Framework is nominally alive but the ceasefire is in name only: Israel besieged and then demolished the Ali al-Taher tunnel complex (about 1,100 tonnes of explosives, a magnitude 4.1 tremor) and declared its security zone 'complete', Hezbollah is waging drone, IED and ATGM attrition, and the Rome round slipped to October behind the 27 Oct Israeli election.
changes: Pilot zones launched 20–22 Jul (Froun and Srifa outside the IDF buffer, Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh inside it; LAF deployed to Zawtar on 21 Jul after an IDF withdrawal); the LAF said Israeli shelling and bulldozing hindered completion (26 Jul) and on 9 Sep claimed control of all three zones with ~1,818 weapons seized (~86% light ammunition), with near-daily LAF–Hezbollah coordination and no depot dismantlement (FDD).

The ceasefire effectively broke down on 15–16 Aug (Hezbollah drone wounded three Yahalom engineers on Ali al-Taher; IDF strikes on Ansar, Deir al-Zahrani and the ridge killed 11+); repeated LAF-handover formulas failed (Hezbollah's 20 Aug offer refused; Aoun approached Washington 24 Aug); the IDF 36th Division declared operational control on 3 Sep and demolished the 2 km-plus tunnel complex on 10 Sep, after which Katz and Netanyahu declared the security zone 'complete'.

Hezbollah's method shifted from rockets to FPV and one-way drones, IEDs and ATGMs inside the zone (2–4 Sep drones intercepted; a roadside IED wounded two troops); IDF retaliation expanded north of the zone to Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Arab Salim for the first time since June.

A 'Gray Line' plan was reported on 7 Sep — an IDF pullback to 2–4 km inside Lebanon, vacating Beaufort and Ali al-Taher — but it is not politically approved; the Rome round was postponed to October (UNGA, holidays, the Paris LAF meeting), ambassadors met at the State Department on 15–16 Sep on pilot-zone expansion, and a Paris preparatory meeting (Macron, Aoun, King Abdullah) was held on 17 Sep; Israel released five Lebanese detainees via US mediation on 3 Sep.

Costs: Lebanese Health Ministry counts 4,386 killed and 12,407 wounded since 2 Mar (8,953 since October 2023) with 360,000 still displaced (UNHCR, Aug); Israel lost 37 soldiers and 4 civilians in the 2026 round by late July. Singapore exposure lowered to Low: no shipping or energy channel and no evidence of a regional-partner ask through the Military Coordination Group.

history.note: Washington Framework signed; Military Coordination Group may seek regional partners; fighting continues.

timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Lebanese army troops deployed in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first of three US-supervised pilot zones, after Israeli forces pulled back from the village.
Israeli air strikes killed at least four people around Nabatieh after Israel said Hezbollah launched two drones at its troops in south Lebanon.

Incidents without fire: PM Anutin visited troops on Hill 500 (23 Aug; Cambodia protested 'illegal occupation'); a Thai helicopter crossed ~400 m into Battambang airspace (3–4 Sep, Cambodian protest under the Chicago Convention and the December GBC statement); Thailand took the ASEAN Observer Team into O'Smach (7 Sep), which Cambodia called an unlawful assertion of authority.

Resistance drone warfare crossed a threshold: six fibre-optic FPV drones struck Tada-U airbase (Mandalay) on 10 Sep, the first strike on a fighter base; the KIA destroyed ~25 Irrawaddy supply vessels since late August and wiped out a 130-man Bhamo breakout column (12–14 Sep). Adaptation raised to High.

Politics: President Min Aung Hlaing's 100-day peace-talks deadline (31 Jul) passed with KNU, CNF and ABSDF rejection; state visits to China, Thailand and Vietnam; ASEAN (59th AMM, Manila) kept non-political representation and demanded 'demonstrable progress' — Singapore's foreign minister: 'not enough progress'; UN credentials contest ahead.

history.note: FPV strike on Tada-U airbase, failed junta Rakhine offensive and AA counter-offensive, ASEAN seat decision pending.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government at the parliament complex in Naypyitaw.
Min Aung Hlaing offers peace talks to armed groups with a 100-day deadline ending 31 July; the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and National Unity Government reject it.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Min Aung Hlaing begins a three-day state visit to Vietnam, his third ASEAN member visit, seeking to normalise ties with the bloc that bars him from its summits.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.
Simultaneous Myanmar Air Force strikes on Ponnagyun, Pauktaw, Gwa and Minbya townships in Rakhine kill at least two civilians and injure three.

items.whyNow: Moved up to Priority: the Houthis ended the 2022 truce, seized the full Red Sea coast including Perim and the Hanish islands (3–11 Sep), and cut Bab al-Mandab transits to ~12 a day; a Singapore-flagged VLCC has already diverted; Iraqi militia drones shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline while the US leaves Iraq by 30 Sep.
changes: Houthis declared the 2022 truce over and a 'naval blockade' of Saudi Arabia (20 Jul); ballistic missiles killed six on the Egyptian cargo ship Tihamah in Bab al-Mandab (11 Aug, first fatal ship attack since February) and hit a Bahri tanker off Yanbu (24 Aug); 12 attacks or attempts since July.

3–11 Sep offensive took Mocha, Hays, Khawkhah, the Hanish islands and Perim — the whole Red Sea coast; Lloyd's List transits fell from ~30 to ~12 a day, Brent above $100, Asia–Europe rates up 25–40%; Trump reportedly declined a Saudi request for air support; Saudi two-week ceasefire offer via Oman and US–Houthi talks in Muscat (18 Sep), no Houthi reply yet.

Iraq: PMF drones on Saudi oil (27–29 Jul) drew US–Saudi strikes on the PMF in seven provinces (29 Jul, 20+ killed); drones from Maysan shut the East-West pipeline (5m b/d) on 11–12 Sep; Patriots withdrawn from Erbil (5 Aug) and remaining US troops leave by 30 Sep, mostly to Jordan; Baghdad recast the 30 Sep militia disarmament deadline as the 'start of a process'.

Israel–Syria: 26 Jul incursion and checkpoint at Al-Ardah, eight strikes on Abu al-Duhur airbase (17–18 Aug, Turkish deployment cited), 267 violations in August; Jordan-hosted security talks (24 Aug) proposed a US-supervised operations room and Sharaa calls a deal 'progressing'; Katz: Israel will not leave Hermon or the buffer zone.

history.note: Baseline: dormant after the Red Sea lull.
Houthi Red Sea ban reinstated 8 June.
Houthis seized the Red Sea coast and cut Bab al-Mandab transits to ~12/day; Saudi pipeline shut by Iraqi militia drones; US leaving Iraq.

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says 30 September is the 'fixed and final' date for ending the US-led coalition mission and completing the withdrawal of its forces.
Israel strikes Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, saying it aims to prevent a Turkish military deployment; Damascus and Ankara deny the claim.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.
Ship transits through Bab al-Mandab halve to 15 from 30 the previous day, according to Kpler data, as the Houthi advance raises Red Sea risk.
The Houthis fire a ballistic missile and drones at Riyadh for the first time in this escalation; Saudi Arabia says it was intercepted as smoke rises near King Khalid airport.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa says in New York that security talks with Israel reached about 90 percent agreement before Israel pulled back, and that negotiations continue.

status.summary: The Houthis have ended their truce with Saudi Arabia, seized the full Red Sea coast including the Bab al-Mandab islands, and cut transits there to about a dozen a day; Saudi Arabia has offered a two-week ceasefire via Oman. Iraqi militia drones shut Saudi Arabia's main east–west pipeline in mid-September as the last US troops leave Iraq, and Israel keeps striking in Syria while a security deal is negotiated.
